name: All Fours (17th Century)
description: This is the earliest documented form of All Fours, as described in Charles Cotton's 'The Compleat Gamester' (1674). It laid the foundation for dozens of American and British trick-taking games, introducing the iconic 'Begging' mechanic and the four-point scoring system.

overview.description: This is the earliest documented form of All Fours, as described in Charles Cotton's 'The Compleat Gamester' (1674). It laid the foundation for dozens of American and British trick-taking games, introducing the iconic 'Begging' mechanic and the four-point scoring system.

history.origins: All Fours originated in Kent, England, and was famously denounced as a 'common' or 'vulgar' game by high society, despite its deep tactical complexity.
timeline: 1674: First published rules in Charles Cotton's 'The Compleat Gamester'.
1700s: Spreads to the American colonies, becoming the progenitor of 'Pitch' and 'Old Sledge'.
1800s: Evolution into 'Seven Up' in the United States.
history.cultural: Cotton noted the game was 'much played in Kent' and characterized it by the 'Begging' for trumps.
history.evolution: The 17th-century rules are strictly for 2 players. Later 19th-century variants added partnership play and expanded the scoring targets.

setup.dealing: Each player receives 6 cards in batches of 3. The 13th card is turned up to set the potential trump suit.
setup.equipment: Standard deck, counters or tokens for 11 points.

rules.objective: Be first to the agreed game total (commonly 11) by collecting High, Low, Jack, and Game points.
rules.gameplay: Deal six cards each in packets of three and turn up the next card for proposed trump. If the non-dealer accepts, play proceeds. If the non-dealer begs, the dealer either gifts one point and throws in the hand immediately, or runs cards by dealing three more each and turning again until trump suit changes. In trick play, players may always play trump, but cannot play off-suit non-trump when able to follow suit. Highest trump wins; if no trump is played, highest of led suit wins. After play, score points in order High, Low, Jack, Game.
keyRules: High (1 pt): Held by the player dealt the highest trump.
Low (1 pt): Held by the player dealt the lowest trump.
Jack (1 pt): Awarded to the player who WINS the Jack of trumps in a trick.
Game (1 pt): Awarded to the player with the highest 'pip' total in their captured tricks (Ace=4, King=3, Queen=2, Jack=1, 10=10).
A gift after a beg ends the hand immediately and deals pass.

strategy.basic: If you have an Ace of any suit, you have a strong chance for 'Game' points since Aces are worth 4. Protect your Tens!
strategy.intermediate: The Beg: If you have no trumps or only middle trumps (e.g., 7 or 8), always Beg. You risk giving the dealer a point, but you might find a better suit where you hold the Ace or Two.
strategy.advanced: Lead Management: Since the Jack point is awarded to the winner of the trick (not the holder), use your high trumps to 'fish' for the opponent's Jack if you suspect they have it.
tips: Remember: 'Low' is scored by the person who was DEALT the card, not the one who wins it. You can lose the Two of trumps in a trick and still get the 'Low' point.
Winning the 10 of any suit is half the battle for the 'Game' point.

variations.name: Running All Fours
variations.description: Historical line to 31 where turned trump A/K/Q/J awards dealer 4/3/2/1 at deal time.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Running All Fours is noted as a scoring extension of this ruleset; engine-level differences beyond target score are not yet modelled here.

scoring.description: Points are scored 1-by-1 at the end of the hand.
scoring.winCondition: First player to 11 points wins (or other agreed target).
